chunks: Ibn Abi Umayr from Ali al-Sayrafī from al-Mufaddal ibn 'Umar al-Ju'fī said:

I was with Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) when dirhams were thrown before him, so he threw one dirham to me and said, 'What is this?' I said, 'Sattūq.' He said, 'And what is Sattūq?' I said, 'Two layers of silver and a layer of copper and a layer of silver.' He said, 'Break it, for the sale of this is not permissible, nor its spending.'

The point in this report is that the spending of these dirhams is not permissible unless it is clarified that they are so, because whenever it is not clarified, the one who takes it will assume they are good (pure), and that which reveals what we mentioned is what he narrated.

key_terms.سَتُّوقٌ: A type of composite coin with layers of precious and base metals
key_terms.لاَ إِنْفَاقُهُ: Nor its spending (using it as currency)
key_terms.لاَ يَحِلُّ بَيْعُ هَذَا: The sale of this is not permissible

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on spending composite or layered coins like Sattūq in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the principle of *gharar* (uncertainty) in commercial transactions, specifically regarding composite currency like 'Sattūq' dirhams. The Imam instructs breaking the coin to reveal its true silver content, ensuring that the buyer is not deceived by the appearance of purity when the base metal layer is hidden. This establishes a practical precedent for verifying the intrinsic value (*qimah*) of mixed assets before trade or expenditure.
